verdict: The dialect work is genuinely good and I want to say so before the damage report: moyn, gyda/'da, sdim, tamed bach, mas/lan/bant, tad-cu and mam-gu, twym, clou, brwnt, becso, llefain, cwympo, hewl, bord, ffwrn, winwns, whare, gweud, ishte, dishgled, ontefe, jiw jiw and yffach are all the right calls, the mutation notes are accurate far more often than not, and localisation decisions like maes awyr at tier 4, cwrw and rygbi at tier 2 and hiraeth at tier 2 show real judgement about life in Wales. Three systemic problems undercut it. First, the Hindi spine is still visible in roughly thirty notes - the paneer slot, the khichdi slot, the okra slot, the sari slot, "same role as raita", "no lakh here", "in place of Hindi's biryani" - which is scaffolding a paying learner must never see, and in two places (hs-0024's "Oh I see", hs-0229's "seems/takes an hour", hs-0137's "near") the leftover has displaced the note the Welsh word actually needed. Second, this is not 1,154 teachables: I count 80-plus duplicate or near-duplicate headwords (cawl three times, tacsi three times, i fi three times, modryb four times, ffan and the wedi-perfect and the conjugated-preposition paradigm twice each), the duplicates carry conflicting tiers and conflicting spellings (sos coch vs saws coch, gymrwch vs gymerwch, sai'n vs sa i'n, Dewch i mewn vs Dewch mewn), one id is used twice (hs-0385) and one is missing (hs-0770) - so the real distinct count is nearer a thousand and the tier-2 band is padded with its own tier-1 items re-listed. Third, and most tellingly, the things a Hindi spine had no reason to generate are exactly what's absent: croeso (the reply to every diolch, nowhere in the list), the nasal and aspirate mutations as their own cards while soft mutation gets one, the Oes/Ydy question split, the negative past, question formation at all, gartre/adre, tegell, peint, cwtsh, chwarae teg, talu, ci, age, job names, spring and snow, and above all any way to ask a Welsh speaker not to switch to English - which is the single most-needed sentence in a learner's first year in Wales. The outright errors are few but they sit on flagship items: hs-0007 and hs-0094 illustrate the southern yw with the northern "Ydy e'n dod?", hs-1126 illustrates hiraeth with Nain, hs-0550 calls tywallt southern, hs-0074 and hs-0155 illustrate aspirate mutation with "â chi" where nothing mutates, hs-0581 and hs-1056 present bare verb-nouns as imperatives, and hs-0084 teaches "bare stem" for the ti imperative when regular verbs take stem + -a and every example given is an irregular. Strip the Hindi, merge the duplicates, fix those seven, add the thirty-odd missing essentials, and this is a shipping southern-Welsh syllabus.

'sglods' in speech. 'pysgod a sglodion' – fish and chips.
'creision ŷd' – cornflakes.
Grefi ar bopeth; the default with cinio dydd Sul. (Note said 'same role as raita'.)
Literally 'red sauce'; brown sauce is 'saws brown'.
'rhy hallt' – too salty. 'dŵr hallt' – sea water.
South's word; north says 'cacen'. 'teisen pen-blwydd'.
'hufen' alone is cream.
'ewin o arlleg' – a clove of garlic.
Literally 'flower cabbage'.
Singular 'cenhinen'. The national vegetable, in every pot of cawl and on the lapel on Dydd Gŵyl Dewi. 'cennin Pedr' are daffodils.
Bresych a thatws; bresych coch = red cabbage. (Note said 'fills the okra slot'.)
'pys slwtsh' – mushy peas.
Singular 'moronen'. Vegetables are usually collective in Welsh, with a singular in -en.
Spinach isn't a fixture here; the leafy green in a Welsh fridge is lettuce.
Saws persli with ham is the traditional pairing. (Note said 'the coriander slot'.)
'leim' for lime.
Literally 'wine grains'.
'halen a phupur' – salt and pepper. Same word for the vegetable.
'sbeisys' for spices.
'powdwr tsili'.
'sudd oren' – orange juice.
What the children get; 'diod oren' does the same job.
Peint o gwrw; cwrw casgen = real ale. Essential for the pub and the club. (Note said 'the Hindi list has no room for'.)
'pop' is the everyday word; 'diod ffisi' the descriptive one.
'llaeth sur' – sour milk; also used of a person's mood.
'poeth' also does 'hot' in the chilli sense.
Re-tiered up: you'll want it at every meal with family. Spoken alternatives 'hyfryd' and 'lyfli'.
'dim blas arno' – no taste to it.
For undercooked food people usually just say 'heb goginio'n iawn'.
'llysieuol' – vegetarian; 'llysieuwr/llysieuwraig' the person.
'berwi'r tegell' – boil the kettle, the most-used sentence in the house.
Huge word: cut, chop, break, cut hair, 'torri syched' – quench a thirst.
'bwydo'r plant', 'bwydo'r gath'.
Tea-making staple. 'Dwy lwyaid' – two spoonfuls.
Or just 'Bwyd!' shouted up the stairs.
chi-form 'Golchwch eich dwylo'. Soft mutation after 'dy': dwylo becomes ddwylo.
South 'twymo'; north 'cynhesu'.
No filtering ritual here – tap water is what's drunk and offered.
Plural 'cyllyll'.
South 'ffwrn'; north 'popty'. 'yn y ffwrn' – in the oven.
'tun' for a tin; 'blwch' is the formal word.
Full form 'ystafell wely'; the initial y drops in speech. Soft mutation: gwely becomes wely after the feminine noun.
South also says 'rŵm ffrynt' for the front room.
Yn yr ardd; gardd gefn = back garden, garddio = gardening. (Note said 'the balcony slot'.)
'nenfwd' is the ceiling inside.
South says 'staer': 'lan staer' – upstairs, 'lawr staer' – downstairs.
'ar lawr' – on the floor; 'lawr' also means down.
South also 'iet' or 'giât'. 'Caewch y gât' – shut the gate, said on farms daily.
'cloi' – to lock; 'dan glo' – locked up.
'cloch y drws'. Also in telling time: 'o'r gloch'.
'gobennydd' is the bed pillow proper, but 'clustog' is what most people say.
'carthen' is the traditional woven Welsh blanket, still on plenty of beds.
Gwybed mân = midges, a real problem on a summer evening; cleren = a fly (South). (Note said 'mosquitoes aren't a thing here'.)
'gwydr' is glass the material.
'ysgub' is the formal word for a broom.
'mwg o de'. Careful: 'mwg' also means smoke.
'rwbish' just as common in speech, and means nonsense too.
'rho fe yn y bin'. Bin day is 'diwrnod y biniau'.
'twtio' – to tidy up.
'sychu' – to dry, to wipe.
'Mae'n wlyb heddi' – weather small talk you'll use constantly.
'peiriant golchi llestri' – dishwasher.
Literally 'the gadget' – what everyone calls it. 'rimôt' also heard.
Spoken loan; the formal term 'gwefrydd' is rarely said out loud.
'switsio' – to switch.

items.en: to light, to put on (a light or fire)
items.note: 'cynnau'r tân'. For appliances people say 'rhoi ymlaen'.
'wedi malu' – broken, knackered, of anything from a kettle to a car. 'malu awyr' – to talk rubbish.
The Welsh-house version of the geyser line. 'y gwres' – the heating.
Clipped from 'Does dim'. South 'twym'; north 'poeth'.

items.word: Wyt ti wedi diffodd y nwy?
items.roman: Wyt ti wedi diffodd y nwy?
items.en: did you turn the gas off?
items.note: 'diffodd' – to switch off, put out.
'torri gwallt' – to have a haircut.
Plural 'clustiau'; 'clustog' the cushion comes from it.
Plural 'dannedd'; 'dannedd gosod' – false teeth.
Organ and feeling both. ''nghalon i' – my love, said to a child.
'Mae 'nghefn i'n gwynegu' – my back's aching. Prime doorstep conversation.
'prawf gwaed' – blood test.
For 'mind' use 'meddwl'.
'anadlu' – to breathe; 'mas o wynt' – out of breath.
'Mae'r bendro arna i' – I'm dizzy. Another of the 'ar' ailments.
'Dw i'n teimlo'n wan'. Also of tea.
Everyday speech prefers 'wedi brifo' or south 'dolur'.
'trafferth 'da'r cefn' – trouble with my back; 'dim trafferth' – no bother.
'Mae'n brifo' – it hurts. South also uses 'dolur' as the noun.
Most people say 'y cemist'.
Illnesses sit 'on' you in Welsh: annwyd, ofn, cywilydd, y ffliw.
'ers' – since, for (a stretch of time up to now).
'ers dyddiau' – for days. 'deuddydd' is the tidy two-day word.
'taflu lan' is the colloquial 'throw up'.
South possession ''da fi'; north 'gen i'.
'Mae e wedi brifo'i hunan' – he's hurt himself.
South 'nawr'; north 'rŵan'.
More natural than the literal 'gorffwyswch'.
South 'cer'; north 'dos'. chi-form 'Ewch at y doctor'. Note 'at' for going to a person.

items.word: Wyt ti wedi cymryd dy dabledi?
items.roman: Wyt ti wedi cymryd dy dabledi?

items.note: 'cyn bwyd' – before food.
'rhywbeth at annwyd' – something for a cold. 'at' for what a medicine is for.
'yr un 'na' – that one; 'yr un fach' – the little one (feminine takes the soft mutation).
South 'twym'; north 'poeth'. Weather: 'Mae'n dwym heddi'.
Same word as the fruit.
Of people and behaviour: 'paid bod yn gas'. 'gwael' and 'drwg' cover bad in other senses.
'tal' for a tall person. 'cyn bo hir' – before long.
'trwchus' for thick things like a book or fog.
South's everyday word; standard and north 'cyflym'. 'Dere glou!' – come quick!
Feminine 'trom'. 'glaw trwm' – heavy rain.
Said 'sgafn' in speech.
In speech often just 'Ble ti'n mynd?' with no 'i'.
'wrth bwy' when it's telling or saying: 'wrth bwy wedest ti?'
Said ''da pwy' in the south. Aspirate mutation: pwy becomes phwy after gyda.
'erbyn' – by (a deadline): 'erbyn dydd Llun'.
'Pa mor hir?' also works.
Doubles as 'what do you think?' – tone and context separate them.
hwn/hwnna (m), hon/honna (f), rhain/rheina (pl). Point and say it.
South 'i fi'; north 'i mi'. The set runs i fi, i ti, iddo fe, iddi hi, i ni, i chi, iddyn nhw.
Clipped 'gyda fe'. South's possession: 'Mae car 'da fe' – he's got a car.
Feminine 'iddi hi'. 'Rho fe iddo fe' – give it to him.
'rhywbeth arall' – something else; 'rhywle arall' – somewhere else.
'dal i' for still doing: 'dw i'n dal i aros'.

items.en: the question / relative / near / far grid
items.note: Ask with ble, pryd, shwd, pwy; link with lle, pan, fel, sy. (Used 'sut' where the whole syllabus teaches shwd.)
'o flaen y tân' – in front of the fire.
'yng nghanol' – in the middle of. 'rhyngon ni' – between us.
In speech 'am' does it: 'mynd am Gaerdydd'.
Nasal mutation after 'yn': tŷ becomes nhŷ. South also says 'draw 'da Siân'.
'mwy na' – more than. Aspirate mutation after 'na': llai na thri.
'neu fel arall' at the front of a warning.
Also the answer to thanks, like 'not at all'.
'Mae'n edrych fel glaw' – looks like rain.
Literally 'little people'. The all-purpose surprised exclamation.
'Diolch o galon' – heartfelt thanks.
The everyday spoken form. Fuller: 'mae'n ddrwg 'da fi' (south) / 'gen i' (north).
Spoken clipping of 'edrychwch'; ti-form 'drycha'.
'gormod' – too much; 'gormod o waith'.

items.en: all of it, the whole lot
items.note: Follows its noun: 'y bwyd i gyd', 'pawb i gyd'. 'y cyfan' is the tidier written option.
What people actually say; 'llawer o' is the formal one. Soft mutation after 'o': lot o bobol.
'troi'n' also does it: 'mae'r tywydd wedi troi'n oer'.
'rhaid i fi' + soft mutation on the verb: mynd becomes fynd.
Tagged on the end: 'mae e gartre, siŵr o fod'.
'cael hoe fach' – to have a little breather, more spoken.
'yn barod' – ready.

items.word: Siaradwn ni eto cyn bo hir
items.roman: Siaradwn ni eto cyn bo hir

items.note: 'Dw i ar fin gadael' – I'm just about to leave.
'mynd nôl' – to go back.
mynd i weld Mam, mynd i siopa, dod i gael te. Soft mutation after 'i': gweld becomes weld.
Often just 'mae'n bwrw'. Heavier: 'mae'n arllwys' or 'pistyllio'. Wales's most-used sentence.
Spoken loan; 'archebu' is the formal word.

items.en: could I have a word with ...?
items.note: Used to ask for someone on the phone or at the door.
'tacsi' is the general word; outside the cities it's a phone call to the local firm.
No underground, but do not say the word doesn't exist here: the Valley Lines are being rebuilt and branded Metro De Cymru, so it is on signs and in the news. Day to day: y bws, y trên.
'darllen y mesurydd' – to read the meter.
'gyrru' – to drive, and also to send.
'bag am oes' – bag for life.
Usually said as 'mae'r traffig yn ofnadwy'.
'ciwio' – to queue.
In practice people just say 'cerdded': 'cerdded i'r dre'.
'Pa mor ...?' builds any 'how + adjective' question: pa mor hir, pa mor ddrud.
Soft mutation after 'pa': platfform becomes blatfform.
South 'odi' for 'ydy'.
'gwerth am arian' – value for money; 'gwerth chweil' – worthwhile.
'cash' is said just as often.
Most people say 'contactless' or 'talu ar y ffôn'.
Also a bank of earth, and 'twll yn y wal' is the cashpoint.
'hanner pris' – half price; 'bargen' – a bargain.
Clipped from 'Does dim newid gyda fi'.
Nearly always just 'y ffôn'.
'grŵp y teulu' – the family group chat.
'sdim signal 'ma' – no signal here, a real problem in the valleys.

items.word: Alla i ddim dy weld di
items.roman: Alla i ddim dy weld di
items.note: 'mae'r llun wedi rhewi' – the picture's frozen.
'wedyn' – afterwards, later on.
Same fault as hs-0581: 'Agor y ffenest' is the verb-noun. ti: agora'r ffenest; chi: agorwch y ffenest.
South Wales staple, mild but not for chapel. 'Yffach gols!' is the full version.
'ffantastig' and 'grêt' do the same job in speech.
The resigned or wrapping-up shrug, from 'dyna ni'. Consoling and closing both.
The standard answer to 'beth ti'n neud?'
'digon' – enough; 'teg' – fair.
South prefers 'ffeindio' to the formal 'dod o hyd i'.
Can mil = a hundred thousand; miliwn, biliwn. (Note said 'no lakh here'.)
The Welsh-language institution behind the singing, the funerals and half the social calendar. 'eglwys' is the church.
South says 'yn grac' for cross: 'mae Mam yn grac'.
Another 'ar' state, like annwyd and cywilydd.
'chwerthin am ben rhywun' – to laugh at someone.
South's word; north and standard 'crio'.
Also the noun 'change' (money).
'gad lonydd iddo' – leave it alone; chi-form 'Gadewch e'.
'cân' – a song. Also 'to ring': 'mae'r ffôn yn canu'. You will need this one in Wales.
After the noun it means lonely, before it means only: 'yr unig un' – the only one.
Everyday, not blasphemous. South also 'sa i'n gwbod, wir' – I really don't know.
Only the first five are irregular (cyntaf, ail, trydydd, pedwerydd, pumed). Feminine forms differ for third and fourth: y drydedd, y bedwaredd.
'chwarter i wyth'. Soft mutation after 'i'.
'wrth y goleuadau' – at the lights.
'ffonio 999'.
'têcawe' – a takeaway.
'tro i'r chwith' – turn left. Also 'to turn into': 'troi'n oer'.
'y lle mae Mam yn byw' – where Mam lives. 'ble' also does this job in speech.
From 'gwneud y tro'. 'digon da' – good enough.
The resigned shrug in question form.
The standard word; 'iwso' is the spoken one.
For nil or nothing you say 'dim': 'dim i ddim' – nil-nil.
'cant a hanner' also heard. 'can' before a noun: 'can punt'.
Feminine 'pedwaredd': y bedwaredd flwyddyn.
Literally 'week's end'. 'penwythnos diwetha' – last weekend.

items.word: y cynta o Fai, yr ail o Fehefin
items.roman: y cynta o Fai, yr ail o Fehefin
items.note: Every date takes an ordinal: y cynta o Fai, y pymthegfed o Awst. Soft mutation on the month after o: Mai becomes Fai. (Note said 'unlike Hindi'.)
ym mis Ionawr - in January: yn becomes ym before m. (The old note read 'mis becomes mis with ym', which says nothing.)
Same word as Tuesday: 'dydd Mawrth' is the day, 'mis Mawrth' the month.
Eisteddfod month – the first full week of August.
Also the verb 'to reap' – it's harvest month.
Also means autumn.
How a man refers to his wife: 'mae'r wraig yn dod'. 'y gŵr' for the husband.
Usually said as 'maen nhw wedi dyweddïo' – they've got engaged.
'priodferch' – bride.
'yr henoed' is the collective term used by services and the chapel.
Goes before its noun and softens it: 'hen ddyn'. Affectionate in 'yr hen Dai'; 'hen bryd' – about time.
Male glanhawr. A cleaner once a week is as far as household help goes here. (Note framed it against Hindi live-in help.)
Plural 'esgyrn'. 'asgwrn cefn' – backbone.
'cymer flas' – have a taste.
Butchers and markets here still work in pounds: 'hanner pwys o gig'.
'ffwrn' is the oven part; many say 'hob' for the rings.
'bag am oes' – bag for life, and you pay for one if you forget it.
Mae'r boeler wedi torri is a sentence you will need in January; boeler combi, gwasanaethu'r boeler. (Note called it 'the equivalent of the geyser'.)
'chwysu' – to sweat.
For getting on a bus it's 'mynd ar y bws'.
'Prynhawn da' after midday, 'Noswaith dda' in the evening.
Parting only, never a greeting. 'Cysga'n dawel' – sleep well.
The host's offer. Informally: 'Ti moyn paned?' – south uses 'moyn' for want.
'Shwmae, ers talwm!' is the standard reunion greeting. 'ers talwm' on its own means 'in the old days'.
South 'becso'; north 'poeni'. chi-form 'Peidiwch becso'. 'Paid becso dim' – don't worry at all.

items.en: hiraeth, longing for home or someone gone
items.note: mae hiraeth arna i am Mam-gu. ('Nain' is the northern word - wrong in a southern syllabus, and this is the flagship Welsh item.) For plain missing someone the South says gweld ishe: dw i'n gweld dy ishe di.
'Dw i'n brysur' – I'm busy.
'Wyt ti'n rhydd nos Wener?'. Free of charge is 'am ddim'.
'gwaith' is work in general. Also in county names: Sir Gaerfyrddin.
'astudio' – to study; 'ysgol' – school.
'prifysgol' – university.
In practice people name it: Pobol y Cwm on S4C is the one everyone has an opinion about.
'y gêm' with no further explanation means the rugby. 'gêm rygbi', 'gêm bêl-droed'.
'Newyddion S4C' at seven. 'newydd' – new.
'ffonio'r feddygfa' – ring the surgery, at eight on the dot for an appointment.
Plural 'pengliniau'.
'dal hwn' – hold this; 'dal y bws'. Also 'still': 'dw i'n dal 'ma'.
South's word; north 'syrthio'. 'mae e wedi cwympo' – he's had a fall.
'estyn y llaeth i fi' – pass me the milk. The table verb.
'unrhyw beth' – anything; 'unrhyw le' – anywhere.
bydda i, byddi di, bydd e, byddwn ni, byddwch chi, byddan nhw. Negative 'fydd e ddim'.
Dw i ar fin gadael, mae hi ar fin dechrau. South also uses 'jyst â' for almost: 'dw i jyst â starfo'.
'gwna fe'n iawn' – do it properly. Same phrase as 'fine, all right'.

items.en: have a bite before you go
items.note: South 'tamed' for 'tamaid'. Nobody leaves a Welsh kitchen unfed.

items.en: ring me when you get there
items.note: 'rho ganiad i fi' – give me a ring, very Welsh.
'Da iawn chi' to more than one or to an elder. 'Campus!' and 'Bendigedig!' are stronger praise.
South's word; north 'del'. 'bach' does cute: 'babi bach pert'.
Shoes off at the door is normal here too.
The festival everyone talks about, local or national. 'Dydd Gŵyl Dewi' on 1 March is the other fixture in the calendar.
The spoken southern default: 'wyt ti'n iwso hwn?'. 'defnyddio' is the standard word.
'pen-blwydd' alone is a birthday.
'sbectol haul' – sunglasses.
Missing entirely, yet it's the reply to every diolch: Diolch. – Croeso. Also croeso i Gymru, croeso mawr, mae croeso i ti.
The everyday refusal at a Welsh table, where food is offered three times. Warmer: dim i fi, diolch.
Two words where English has one: mae hi gartre (staying), dw i'n mynd adre (moving). Written gartref/adref. Both appear in other notes but neither is taught.
The sentence that buys patience. Feminine dysgwraig. Soft mutation after yn: dysgwr becomes ddysgwr.

chi: peidiwch â newid i'r Saesneg. Softer: dal ati yn Gymraeg 'da fi, plîs. Welsh speakers switch the second they hear a learner - this is the day-one survival phrase and no Hindi-derived list would ever produce it.

items.word: Wyt ti'n ...? / Ych chi'n ...? / Yw e'n ...?
items.roman: Wyt ti'n ...? / Ych chi'n ...? / Yw e'n ...?
items.note: South: Yw e'n dod? or Odi hi'n dod? (Ydy is North/standard). With ti, speech usually just uses intonation: Ti'n dod? Answer by echoing the verb: Ydw, Odi, Nag ydw. The syllabus teaches the answers (hs-0094) but never the question.

items.en: two ways to ask 'is there' / 'is it'
items.note: Oes with something indefinite (Oes bara 'da chi? – Oes), Yw/Ydy with something definite (Yw'r siop ar agor? – Ydy). The commonest learner slip in Welsh, and it decides which yes you get back.

items.en: nasal mutation: p t c b d g → mh nh ngh m n ng
items.note: Only after fy and yn: fy nhŷ, fy nghar, fy mrawd, fy nyled; yng Nghaerdydd, ym Mangor, yn Nolgellau. Soft mutation gets its own card (hs-0244) but the other two live only in scattered notes.

items.en: aspirate mutation: p t c → ph th ch
items.note: Only three letters, and only after a (and), â/gyda, tri, chwe, ei (her), na, tua: mynd â char, ei chartre hi, gwell na choffi, tua thri.
The negative past is nowhere in the list. South: nes i ddim + verb-noun works for any verb; also es i ddim, weles i ddim byd. 'Haven't': dw i heb fynd.

items.word: dy garu di / ei weld e
items.roman: dy garu di / ei weld e
items.en: a pronoun object of a verb-noun becomes a possessive
items.note: Not caru ti but dw i'n dy garu di; not gweld e but alla i ddim ei weld e; not clywed chi but eich clywed chi. Loose speech does say clywed fi, but you'll hear the tidy form from family all day.
South 'sen i (= taswn i); bydden i'n lico just as common. Softer than dw i moyn, which is what you want when accepting something from a mother-in-law.
Named in two notes but never taught. Dere ma' am gwtsh. Also a cubbyhole: cwtsh dan stâr.
Heard constantly, in Welsh and in English. Chwarae teg iddi – fair play to her. South says whare deg.
Ga i beint, plîs? Soft mutation after ga i. Peint o gwrw, hanner o lager. The syllabus teaches tafarn and cwrw but not how to order.
Rho'r tegell 'mlaen. The list teaches paned, dishgled, mwg and berwi'r tegell in a note, but not the kettle itself.
Plural cŵn; cath = cat; anifail anwes = pet. There is no animal anywhere in 1,154 items, and half of doorstep conversation in Wales is somebody's dog.
Babi bach; mae babi 'da nhw – they've had a baby. Plentyn and plant are taught, babi isn't.
Talu â cherdyn, talu ag arian parod. Faint sy arna i i chi? – how much do I owe you? Shopping is well covered except for paying.
Soft mutation after am: Beth am baned? Beth am fynd i'r dre? Appears inside hs-0135's note but is the main way plans get made.
chi: dewch draw. Dere draw am baned rywbryd is the standard neighbourly invitation; draw appears only in notes.
Age is missing entirely. Dw i'n bedwar deg oed; mae hi'n dair oed; naw mis oed. chi: faint yw'ch oed chi?

Signs and addresses are bilingual and the Welsh name is often unrecognisable: Abertawe (Swansea), Casnewydd (Newport), Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen), Aberhonddu (Brecon), Y Fenni (Abergavenny). Soft mutation after i/o: i Gaerdydd, o Gasnewydd.
hs-0420 asks Beth yw'ch gwaith chi? and nothing in the list can answer it. No 'a/an' in Welsh: dw i'n nyrs, dw i'n athro, dw i'n gweithio i'r cyngor.
Haf and gaea are taught; the other two seasons aren't. Hydref is autumn and October both.
Mae'n bwrw eira. Rhew = ice/frost, rhewi = to freeze. Glaw, haul and gwynt are in; snow closes Welsh schools every winter.
Pob hwyl – all the best, at the end of a message or a call.
chi: cofiwch fi at eich mam. The doorstep sign-off in Welsh-speaking Wales; cofion at the end of a note. Buried in hs-0428's note.
1 March: cennin on the lapel, cennin Pedr in the window, a concert in every school. Dydd Gŵyl Dewi Hapus!
Mae 'na broblem; mae 'na rywun wrth y drws. Negative sdim (does dim), question oes. The list teaches the negative and the answer but not the statement.

Chapel life: mynd i'r angladd, y gwasanaeth. Cydymdeimladau – condolences; meddwl amdanoch chi. Priodas is taught and this isn't, though with older Welsh-speaking neighbours it comes round more often.
hs-0436 and hs-1114 both say shops here work in pounds, then teach only cilo. Hanner pwys o gig, dau bwys o datws. Pwyso = to weigh.
